scripts.comment: Click on this block. It moves the turtle 100 steps.

This blue colored 'move' block came from the "Motion" palette to the left. Click on this block. It makes the turtle draw a line in 100 steps. Notice that the turtle is pointing to the right. The turtle always points to the right when coding begins.
Notice the red error message that is generated below the stage area on the right. This occurred because an embroidery stitch was not defined and only 1 stitch was created.

A 'reset' block was moved to this scripting area. This block can be found in the orange "Control" palette on the left. The palette contains the various code blocks, categorized by function (like Motion, Control, Embroidery, etc.). You select and drag these different colored blocks into the scripting area to build your program. The 'reset' block clears the screen and resets the turtle so that it is pointing to the right. Later try different embroidery stitches. They can be found in the green embroidery palette to the left.
Click on this block. It turns the turtle in the direction and amount specified in the block which is 90 degrees.

Snapping the two blocks together creates a list of commands. To duplicate these blocks, right click your mouse to get a drop down menu. In this menu, you will see duplicate, drag and drop to combine the blocks. You will need four of these blocks to make a square.

Clear the screen by clicking on the 'reset' block. Click on the blocks to the left. A square is now on your stage. And the error message is back! The code needs an embroidery stitch. The code is a little repetitive with the 'move' and 'turn' blocks. Let's eliminate that.

To simplify the code, use the 'repeat' block. It can be found in the orange "Control" palette on the left side of the screen. Wrap the repeat block around the 'move' and 'turn' blocks that are repeated. Add a repeat of 4 because this is how many times the block will be executed to make a square.

Execute this code to see a square created on the stage to the right. The code explained... The 'reset' block clears the screen so that you can start fresh. The embroidery stitch block sets the turtle to do a running stitch, Each stitch is 10 steps long. The 'repeat' block executes the code inside it four times. The 'move' block moves the turtle 100 steps in the direction that it is pointing. When you start a new project or reset, the turtle always points to the right. The 'turn' block moves the turtle 90 degrees to the right.

Execute this code to see a square created on the stage to the right. The Stage on the right explained... This is the area where the turtle lives. When you run your code blocks, the turtle moves and turns to follow each command. The turtle always starts at the origin—the point (0,0) in the very center of the stage. By default, it faces to the right, along the X-axis. The embroidery stitch block tells the turtle to make stitches. These stitches are shown on the screen when you run your code. A cross-stitch pattern is shown. Stitches: Shows how many stitches have been created. For example, 128 stitches were made in this design. Jumps: A jump stitch happens when the turtle moves without making any stitches. This is used when the turtle travels from one place to another without stitching in between. In this code, zero jumps occurred. Size: For example, 2.20 x 2.20 cm shows the real size of your design when stitched out. The first number is the width (how wide it is, left to right). This is along the X-axis. The second number is the height (how tall it is, up and down). This is along the Y-axis. If you need to change the size, adjust the move values in your code. Tip: 2 centimeters = about 0.79 inches. If you want to see inches instead of centimeters, look for the turtle icon in the ribbon at the top left. Click the drop-down menu there, and check the box to display measurements in inches. While you are there, check out what else you can do. Below the stage, you will see commands to control how your design looks on the screen. Try the “+” and “–” buttons to zoom in and out. Experiment with the other controls to see what they do. If your code is running slowly, you can turn on Turbo Mode to make it run faster. Finally, there are buttons to export your design: SVG: This format is for graphics (for example, cutting machines or web images). Melco/EXP and Tajima/DST: These are special embroidery files that hold all the stitching instructions for embroidery machines.
